title: Kotl Architecture
intro: Teal is Kotl, our product. Purple is Slurm. Gray is everything else off the shelf, plus the hardware. The dot on each box is its build status; click a box for exactly what's happening.
latest: v1.0.0: Kotl sets up and removes FPGA PCs itself (deploy/kotl/pc.sh), updates everything in one go (deploy/kotl/update.sh), uninstalls completely (deploy/uninstall.sh), and tells users when their VS Code extension or plugins are out of date. Since: lab notes (what worked before, per tool) with a skill per adapter, and FireSim run packages: remote users build on their own PC and run on the boards through Kotl.

steps.name: Welcome
steps.text: New to Kotl? This guide takes you from your account to your first job. Use ‹ › to step through.

steps.name: Account
steps.text: The admin adds you once (kotl-users, Slurm, the sudo rule). Then log in again so your shell has the group.

steps.name: Setup here
steps.text: On the workstation: kotl setup installs Kotl into your Claude Code and VS Code.

steps.name: Setup on your PC
steps.text: On your own PC: fetch the client bundle and run its installer; it reads Kotl over ssh.

steps.name: First job
steps.text: kotl run --eta 5m -- hostname: queued, a board claimed, a job key on its PC, your command runs, the board is freed.

steps.name: Watch
steps.text: The Kotl daemon refreshes a status file every second; the Claude band, the VS Code panel and kotl top show it.

steps.name: Results
steps.text: Each job leaves a private folder: kotl logs, kotl fetch, kotl history.

steps.name: Your tools
steps.text: Run any tool inside kotl run. FireSim gets extra care from the FireSim adapter (driver checks, cleanup, the console).

steps.name: Rules
steps.text: Shared boards: always through Kotl, honest ETAs, release leases.

steps.name: Submit
steps.text: You (or Claude) run kotl run --eta 1h -- ./my-test.sh. Kotl refuses a job without an exit plan: an ETA, and a command that ends by itself.

steps.name: Queue
steps.text: The CLI hands the job to Slurm with sbatch. Slurm orders it by priority and estimates its start from the ETAs ahead of it.

steps.name: Start
steps.text: A board license frees up. Slurm's job starter runs job.sh, which hands over to Kotl's launcher.

steps.name: Claim board
steps.text: The launcher claims an idle, healthy board in the registry, marks it busy, and adds this job's key to the board's PC.

steps.name: Run
steps.text: Your command runs as you, with an ssh-agent holding only the job key: any tool, unchanged (a test script, a bitstream load, a FireSim run). It reaches the board's PC through the key bus.

steps.name: Over ETA
steps.text: Still running past its ETA? Nothing is killed. The notifier (started every minute by a systemd timer) asks Slurm, then tells the owner and their Claude.

steps.name: Hang
steps.text: A guard trips: the owner's --max. The end step stops the simulation, removes the job key, marks the job over max, and tells the owner.

steps.name: Done
steps.text: Normal end: your command exits. The launcher runs the end step (removes the job key, stops what the enabled adapters name), records the result and frees the board for the next job.

steps.name: Results
steps.text: The collect step fills the job folder. Claude runs kotl fetch to pull it to the user's PC.

steps.name: Meanwhile
steps.text: Every 5 minutes Slurm runs Kotl's health check, which probes the board over the SSH path and marks a bad one down.

steps.name: Request
steps.text: You run kotl lease --eta 2h. It goes into the same Slurm queue as every job.

steps.name: Start
steps.text: Your turn: Slurm starts the lease. The launcher claims the board and adds this lease's key to its PC.

steps.name: Work
steps.text: ssh vcu118-pc1 uses your job key; ssh-add /tmp/kotl-keys-$USER/vcu118-pc1 gives it to your tools or any tool. Run what you like.

steps.name: Over ETA
steps.text: Still working past your ETA? You get a notice, and the queue gets new estimates. Nothing is killed.

steps.name: Release
steps.text: kotl release: the end step removes the key, stops simulations left running and frees the board. Slurm's epilog repeats it as a backup.

steps.name: Forgot
steps.text: Walked away? When nothing of yours has run on the PC for the idle time (30m), the launcher ends the lease, frees the board and tells you. --max caps it either way.

steps.name: Request
steps.text: You run kotl board program vcu118-pc1 --bitstream new.bit. It becomes a Slurm job at the admin-only maintenance level.

steps.name: Drain
steps.text: Slurm starts it when it's first in line; the launcher marks PC 1 draining in the registry. A running job there finishes normally, or you cancel it.

steps.name: Program
steps.text: The launcher runs the Program / reset adapter, which loads the bitstream over the kotl SSH path.

steps.name: Verify
steps.text: The board-test adapter checks XDMA with a quick DMA read/write, and the health check confirms the board.

steps.name: Return
steps.text: The registry records the new bitstream and marks PC 1 idle. Users' jobs flow back in, and you get a done notice.

steps.name: Summary
steps.text: What Kotl installs or edits on each machine. Every change is made by a deploy/ script that the admin runs, and each script can undo its own changes.

steps.name: Workstation
steps.text: The workstation carries almost everything: Slurm, MariaDB, the kotl account, Kotl's programs and a few small config snippets.

steps.name: FPGA PC
steps.text: On the PC: a kotl account, one helper script and one sudoers line. sshd stays as it is until full lockdown.

steps.name: Users
steps.text: Nothing system-wide for users; their own tools are only used, never changed.

overview.title: Whole picture
bullets: Teal is Kotl, our product: the code we write and maintain, plus a plugin in each user's Claude.
Purple is Slurm, off the shelf. Kotl talks to it in exactly four places, through its normal commands.
Gray is everything else off the shelf (FireSim, the workstation's OS) and the hardware.
Everything reaching the FPGA PCs goes through the kotl key or a job key that works only while that job runs.

Users keep their own Chipyard and FireSim and run them unchanged inside a generic lease: kotl run -- <command> ends when the command exits, kotl lease ends on release. Kotl enforces an exit plan, not FireSim.
The core is a generic board lease (queue, claim, SSH access, end step). Adapters are admin board care, later: FireSim (flash, recover), program/reset, board tests.
overview.hint: New to Kotl? Open Guides and start with New user: start here. The sidebar lists every part by group; click a group to see what's inside, and a part for what it does, its commands and its files. Progress shows every part by milestone.
overview.tagline: Kotl shares the lab's FPGA boards: every use goes through one queue, gets a board and SSH access only while it runs, and frees the board the moment it ends. Users keep their own tools; Kotl only decides who holds a board, and when.

features.t: One fair queue for every board
features.d: Built on Slurm: one license per board, an ETA on every job to order the queue, urgent and maint priority for the admin. kotl status and kotl top show who holds each board and who waits.

features.t: Access only while your job runs
features.d: Each job gets its own SSH key on the board's PC, added when it starts and removed at its end step. The epilog removes it again if anything is missed. Nothing else gives users a way in.

features.t: Every job has an exit plan
features.d: kotl run frees the board when the command exits; kotl lease on release or after 30 idle minutes; --max (default 2× ETA) stops a hung job. The end step stops only what the job started, never work outside Kotl.
A health check every 5 minutes. A board that fails is held out of the queue (a Slurm reservation) and repaired when it's safe, with notices to the admin. Drain and resume for maintenance.
The core knows nothing about FireSim. The FireSim adapter adds its checks, the XDMA repair, its cleanup and the fsim0 console. Another tool is another adapter.

Build with your own Chipyard anywhere, pack the run (kotl-firesim-pack), copy it to the workstation and run it on a board: Kotl flashes, runs the driver and brings back the results. No FireSim needed on the workstation.
Every job's output, launcher log and status are kept: kotl logs, kotl fetch, kotl history. Notices when your ETA passes, your start slips, or a board goes down or comes back.

Kotl keeps what the lab knows per tool: how the PCs are set up, what works together, a line for every run with what it used (commits, config, bitstream), and signed free notes. Claude reads them before a run and adds what it learned; the paths never change.

features.t: Built for Claude and VS Code
features.d: Every Claude session on the workstation knows Kotl's rules. The plugin adds the skill, the queue at session start and a check before FireSim runs outside Kotl. VS Code shows Kotl in the status bar. Both say when Kotl was updated.
deploy/kotl/pc.sh add sets up a new PC; update.sh updates the workstation and every PC; uninstall.sh removes it all, PCs included. Every step has an --undo and a --dry-run.

kotllens.title: What's Kotl
kotllens.what: Everything highlighted in teal: the code we write, install and maintain.
bullets: Entry: the kotl CLI (run, lease, release, status, fetch), console attach, and the Kotl plugin for Claude Code.

Core: the Kotl daemon (kotld, the one always-running process), the board lease (launcher + PC access), board registry, health check, ETA notifier, job results, the kotl SSH key. Later: power monitor, usage dashboard. Parked: same-design pick.

Adapters: task-specific knowledge, kept out of the core and switched on in kotl.conf. FireSim (built): XDMA and glibc checks, the XDMA repair, its cleanup and console. Later: program/reset, board tests. kotl run and kotl lease work for any tool without them.
kotllens.note: Not Kotl: Slurm (scheduling), each user's FireSim (simulation), the workstation OS (sudo, systemd timers, OpenSSH) and the FPGA PCs. Kotl only uses their normal commands and config files.

slurmlens.title: Where Kotl meets Slurm
slurmlens.what: Four places, numbered like the purple badges. Everything else in Kotl never talks to Slurm.
ordered: Queue ↔ kotl CLI. The CLI submits (sbatch), cancels (scancel) and lists (squeue). Slurm orders the queue by priority and counts boards as licenses.

Job starter → launcher. When a board is free, Slurm runs job.sh, which asks Kotl's launcher to claim it. A cancel arrives as a signal. After the job, Slurm's epilog runs Kotl's end step again as a backup.
Health runner → health check. Slurm runs Kotl's health.sh every 5 minutes.

Accounting → notifier and dashboard. The notifier asks who is running and when queued jobs will start; the dashboard (later) reads history with sacct. The Kotl daemon reads the queue every second (squeue) for the shared status file.
slurmlens.note: Kotl never changes Slurm's code. It only uses Slurm's commands and a few lines of slurm.conf.

remote.title: Remote user PC
remote.what: A user's own machine. Builds happen here; runs happen through the workstation (the FPGA PCs are reachable only from there).
bullets: Builds the design with their own Chipyard and FireSim (bitstream, driver, FireMarshal workload).
Has a normal Linux account on the workstation, reached over SSH, and Kotl's client bundle (Claude plugins, VS Code extension, the adapters' tools).

FireSim from here: kotl-firesim-pack packs the run into a folder, rsync copies it to the workstation, and kotl run … run-package.sh runs it on a board. No FireSim needed on the workstation. (Or keep a Chipyard on the workstation and run FireSim there.)
Never holds a lasting key to the FPGA PCs; a job key works only during their job.
What they get: kotl run and kotl lease for any tool, and Claude knows how to use them.

plugin.title: Kotl plugin for Claude Code
plugin.what: Kotl's plugin for Claude Code. Every user installs it once; Claude then knows how to use the board queue, and sees the queue and your notices when a session starts.
bullets: Skills: the general kotl skill: kotl run (preferred) and kotl lease with an ETA and an exit plan; fetch, then read status.json first; the lab notes; and a table pointing to each tool's own skill. Each adapter brings one (kotl-firesim: read the notes and compare, run FireSim through Kotl with an honest KOTL RESULT and the glibc workaround, then add to the notes). Only the enabled adapters' skills are installed.
SessionStart hook: the queue, the boards and your unread notices (shown, not marked read).
PreToolUse hook (Bash): asks before firesim infrasetup/runworkload/kill runs outside kotl run/lease, and says how to run it through the queue. A suggestion with a question, not a block.

Every Claude session on the workstation, plugin or not: install.sh publishes Kotl's rules as Claude Code's managed /etc/claude-code/CLAUDE.md (use boards only through Kotl; never stop board work that isn't your job's, say who runs it, how long, and that it's outside Kotl). An admin's own file there is left alone.

kotl-band (a second, optional plugin): a live Kotl band above the Claude Code prompt, from the Kotl daemon's status file every second. Collapsed (the default): one short line: each board and its state, how many wait, how many jobs are yours, unread notices, ⚠ and a count when boards have warnings. Expanded: the full status: each board (type, state, the job on it, who, time against ETA and what's left, last health check), the running jobs, everyone waiting in order (who, kind, ETA, estimated start, why), your jobs and notices. Warnings stay a ⚠ count: kotl board list (or Claude) shows them. The ▸/▾ button (or k with the band focused) or /kotl-band expand|collapse switches; the choice is kept across sessions. Read-only.

VS Code extension (kotl.kotl-status): the same in VS Code's status bar, in any window: each board, who holds it and their time of ETA, how many wait, your job count, unread notices; the hover lists the queue with estimated starts and your place in line; a click opens kotl top. Install: code --install-extension /opt/kotl/kotl-status.vsix.
Anywhere: on the workstation it runs kotl; on a user's own PC it runs ssh $KOTL_SSH kotl … (set KOTL_SSH in ~/.claude/settings.json under env).
plugin.note: Convenience only. The SSH lockdown and the end step are the real enforcement.

cli.title: kotl CLI
cli.what: The one command for everything, and generic: it holds a board for whatever you run. It talks to Slurm's queue for you.
bullets: kotl setup installs Kotl into your Claude Code and VS Code (--undo removes it); kotl client-bundle does the same for your own PC.
kotl run --eta T -- CMD: holds a board while CMD runs; ends the moment CMD exits. Good for FireSim runs.
kotl lease --eta T: holds a board for work by hand; ends on kotl release, the idle guard, or --max.
Exit plan, always: the ETA is required, --max defaults to 2× ETA, and a lease always has an idle guard. A job without one is refused.
Inside a job your command gets an ssh-agent holding only the job key, and KOTL_JOB, KOTL_BOARD, KOTL_PC. Your configs aren't touched.
Cancel works only for the job's owner or root.

attach.what: Opens your job's console (a screen session) on its PC, with your job key. Which session comes from the enabled adapter (FireSim: fsim0); with none, the PC's only screen session.
bullets: Runs as you: ssh with only your job key (no agent, no other keys), then screen -x on the adapter's session.
Works only for your own running job, from the workstation (the job key lives there).

launcher.title: Launcher · board lease
launcher.what: The core of Kotl: a generic board lease. It knows nothing about FireSim. Slurm starts it for every job; it claims a board, gives the owner SSH access for the job's lifetime, and always cleans up.
bullets: Confirms the Slurm job is real and belongs to the caller.
Install: sudo deploy/kotl/install.sh --board vcu118-pc1=vcu118@vcu118-pc1 copies the package to /opt/kotl/lib (root-owned) and installs /opt/kotl/launch, the only program users may run as kotl.
Start: claims an idle, healthy board in the registry, then adds this job's key to the board's PC.
During: the owner's command (FireSim, Vivado, scripts, anything) reaches the PC with the job key, through an ssh-agent that job.sh starts for it.
The lease ends when the work ends: the command of kotl run exits (e.g. FireSim's runworkload returns after the simulated Linux powers off), kotl release, or cancel. No timer closes it.
Guards (the exit plan): --max (default 2× ETA) for every job; for a lease also idle: nothing of the PC account running on the PC for N minutes (kotl.conf, 30m).

End step, every time: remove the job key and stop the job's simulations on the PC (in full lockdown: every process of the PC account), record why, free the board. Slurm's epilog repeats it as a backup. A KOTL RESULT: PASS/FAIL line in the output sets the result.
Records setup time on every job, for the parked same-design idea.

Updating Kotl: bash deploy/kotl/update.sh, as the admin. It rebuilds and reinstalls the workstation (install.sh, keeping the boards and adapters), then each board's PC: Kotl's helpers and every enabled adapter's PC part. Users then run kotl setup.

registry.title: Board registry
registry.what: One record per board: its state, what's loaded on it, its health and power.
bullets: States: down → idle → setting up → busy → draining → maintenance → idle.
The launcher claims a board here in one step, so two jobs never share a board.
The health check and power monitor write to it; kotl board list reads it.
A single SQLite file. No service to keep running.

health.title: Health check
health.what: A Kotl script that Slurm runs every 5 minutes. It checks each board over the kotl SSH path.
bullets: Every 5 minutes, one ssh call per PC. Generic: reachable, the board type's card on PCI (VCU118: Xilinx). Each enabled adapter adds its own lines; the FireSim adapter adds XDMA loaded and the glibc version.
Failing on an idle board: each adapter may try one repair (FireSim: one XDMA reload), then the board is checked again. A board a job holds is never touched: its tools may be mid-setup.

Still failing and idle: the board goes down; a Slurm reservation holds its license so queued jobs wait instead of failing; the admin gets a notice. A busy board is never taken from its job: it goes down when the job ends.
Recovery: when the checks pass again the board goes back to idle, the hold is released, and the admin is told.

Warnings (the board stays in the pool): the adapters' (FireSim: glibc differs), and work outside Kotl on an idle board: what runs as the board account, for how long, and who is connected to that PC from the workstation now (from the kernel's connection table). Kotl never stops work outside Kotl; it shows it on kotl board list, kotl top, the band and VS Code.
health.sh always exits 0, so a PC problem never drains the workstation's own Slurm node.

notifier.title: ETA notifier
notifier.what: A short Kotl pass that a systemd timer runs every minute, as kotl. It reads Slurm and writes notices into each user's inbox. It never stops anything.
bullets: Job passes its ETA: the owner hears once. Nothing is stopped.
Job passes 2× its ETA: the owner and the admin hear once.
A queued job's start estimate slips by 15 minutes or more: its owner hears.
Board down or back up: the admin hears (from the health check).
Where: kotl notices, kotl top, the unread count in kotl status, and Claude (M5).

results.title: Job results
results.what: One folder per job, written by the launcher at start and at the end step.
bullets: Owner only (0700, owned by kotl): you read it through the launcher, which checks the job is yours. kotl logs JOB [-f] shows the output; kotl fetch JOB unpacks the whole folder into ./kotl-results/JOB/.
Remote users run the same over SSH (ssh ws kotl fetch JOB); the Claude plugin does it for them.
Other users can't see it. Deleted automatically after 30 days (keep_days in kotl.conf).

lines.c: kotl logs 1235 -f              # follow a running job

power.title: Power monitor
power.what: Reads each board's power on a timer. Never queued, never blocks a job.
bullets: A systemd timer starts it every minute; it reads over the kotl SSH path. No agent on the PCs.
Source to decide later: the board's on-board power sensors, or a smart PDU per PC.
Stores readings in the registry. Alerts if a board draws power while idle, or goes over a limit.

dashboard.title: Usage dashboard
dashboard.what: A small web page on the workstation. Build it once the queue is running.
bullets: Board-hours per user per week, from Slurm's history.
Queue wait times, and how often jobs overrun their ETA.
Board state history and power per board, from the registry.

affinity.title: Same-design pick
affinity.what: On hold: prefer a board that already has the job's bitstream loaded, to save setup time.
bullets: FireSim says to re-run setup before every simulation, so setup can't simply be skipped.
The registry already knows what's loaded, so this would only be a board-pick rule.
Revisit once recorded setup times show it's worth it. No priority boost either way.

fsmod.title: FireSim adapter
fsmod.what: Everything Kotl knows about FireSim, kept out of the generic core. Users still run their own FireSim, unchanged, inside kotl run or kotl lease; this adapter only lets Kotl check, repair and clean up after it.
bullets: Switched on in /etc/kotl/kotl.conf: adapters = firesim (install.sh --adapters firesim). Off, Kotl still runs leases and jobs on any board, with only the generic checks.
Checks (added to the health check's one ssh call): XDMA driver loaded (a failure); glibc on the PC vs the workstation (a warning: drivers built here won't start on an older glibc).

Repair (idle boards only, once per down period): kotl-xdma-reload on the PC loads XDMA exactly as FireSim's infrasetup does (xdma.ko poll_mode=1). Never while a job holds the board: FireSim reloads the driver itself during infrasetup.

End step: stops only what started during the job (the launcher passes the job's age, so the PC's clock doesn't matter): screen sessions fsim* and processes FireSim-* as the board account (matched by process name), then FireSim's root driver with kotl-firesim-stop. Older FireSim work isn't the job's: Kotl leaves it running and logs it as outside Kotl. The epilog does the same if the launcher died.
Lease idle guard: FireSim-* processes count as work.
Console: kotl attach opens screen session fsim0.

User help: /opt/kotl/adapters/firesim/firesim-smoke.sh (installed when the adapter is on) runs infrasetup + runworkload inside kotl run, removes the bundled glibc when the PC's is older (--use-pc-glibc), and prints an honest KOTL RESULT from the uartlog. check.sh confirms a PC works with a user's own FireSim (M1).
Running FireSim: from your own Chipyard, environment active, inside kotl run; the workload must power off by itself. Kotl changes nothing in FireSim or its configs.

Test package (for users without Chipyard): make-test-package.sh builds one self-contained folder (driver and its libraries without the workstation's glibc, bitstream, linux-poweroff workload, run.sh, a README with steps for Claude). kotl run --eta 15m -- <shared folder>/kotl-firesim-test/run.sh checks the PC, flashes the FPGA, boots Linux in screen fsim0, waits for the power-off and prints KOTL RESULT.

Lab notes and skill: a job whose command mentions firesim is a FireSim run: its line in firesim/runs.md carries the FireSim and Chipyard commits, the hardware config, its bitstream and the workload (read as the user, read-only). Its seed text starts setup.md and compatible.md. Its skill, kotl-firesim, is installed with the plugin.

Run packages (FireSim from a Chipyard anywhere, e.g. the user's own PC): kotl-firesim-pack (on the user's PC, from the client bundle) packs what FireSim would copy to the board's PC: the bitstream, the driver and its libraries (not glibc), the workload's boot binary, rootfs and inputs, and the driver's arguments worked out from config_runtime.yaml as FireSim does (checked against the run that passed). The user copies the folder to the workstation; kotl run --eta 20m -- /opt/kotl/adapters/firesim/run-package.sh FOLDER checks the PC (including its glibc against the driver's), flashes, runs the driver in fsim0, brings back the uartlog and outputs (also into the job's results) and prints an honest KOTL RESULT. No FireSim, Chipyard or conda on the workstation. One simulation, no network, VCU118.
Later, admin only: flash a known-good bitstream, recover a board after a crashed job, a short known-good simulation as a deep check.

program.title: Program / reset
program.what: Admin adapter on the lease: load a bitstream or reset a board outside FireSim.

The lease's end step cleans up the same way as for any job.

drvtest.title: Board tests
drvtest.what: Deep check of an FPGA PC and its board, as an adapter on the lease, before the board goes back in the pool.
bullets: Loads the XDMA driver, runs a quick DMA read/write test, records the driver version.
Runs after maintenance, a PC reboot or a failed health check, and optionally on a schedule.
The 5-minute health check stays a quick core probe; this is the thorough one, holding a lease so it never meets a user's job.

key.title: kotl SSH key · job keys
key.what: The only paths from the workstation to the FPGA PCs: Kotl's own key, and short-lived job keys that Kotl adds and removes.
bullets: The kotl private key lives in /home/kotl/.ssh, readable only by the kotl account. Kotl uses it to grant and remove job keys, for health checks and for cleanup.
A job key lets the job's owner and their FireSim into the PC's FireSim account, only while the job runs (see PC access).
FPGA PCs: in full lockdown only kotl, virtex-host (job keys) and the admin, keys only. In soft lockdown (now) virtex-host's password and existing keys still work.
A new PC joins by adding the kotl key, the key helper and a registry entry.

queue.title: Queue + priority
queue.what: Slurm's queue holds waiting jobs and orders them. Kotl's CLI uses it through normal Slurm commands.
bullets: Each board type is a license, counted per board (vcu118:1 today, one board). A job needs one to start.

Priority (rough sketch, tune later): fair-share + waiting time + an "urgent" level only the admin grants. Maintenance has its own admin-only level. Fair-share uses Slurm accounting (slurmdbd + MariaDB on the workstation).
The ETA is required and becomes the job's time limit; Slurm uses it to estimate start times.
Never kills a job for passing its ETA. Only the owner or root can cancel.

starter.title: Job starter
starter.what: The part of Slurm that runs each job and signals it. Here it runs only on the workstation.
bullets: When a board license is free, runs job.sh as the user; it asks Kotl's launcher (as kotl) to claim the board and grant access.
On cancel: sends a stop signal, waits up to 2 minutes (KillWait), then force-stops.
After every job, runs Kotl's epilog: the end step again, as a backup.
Records the job as succeeded or failed from the exit code.

runner.title: Health runner
runner.what: Slurm runs Kotl's health check every 5 minutes. Two lines of slurm.conf.

acct.title: Accounting
acct.what: Slurm's accounting database. Answers who is running, for how long and when queued jobs start, and keeps the history.

os.title: Workstation OS
os.what: The workstation's own Linux pieces that Kotl relies on.
bullets: sudo: one rule lets users run exactly two Kotl programs as kotl.
systemd timers: start the notifier (and later the power monitor) every minute.
OpenSSH: carries the kotl key to the FPGA PCs.
Accounts: users in kotl-users; the kotl service account.
Full list of what Kotl changes here: the System files tab.

pc1.title: VCU118 PC 1
pc1.what: Hosts the lab's VCU118, at 192.168.1.2 (vcu118-pc1 in kotl's SSH config). Reachable only from the workstation.
bullets: Runs sshd, the XDMA driver, FireSim's helper scripts and a small key helper. No other Kotl code.
Accounts: kotl, virtex-host (FireSim; gets job keys) and the admin.

Soft lockdown for now: password logins to virtex-host still work for people who know it. Take a lease (kotl lease) before touching the FPGA, or you may break a running job. Later: full lockdown with a separate admin account.
Reboots are harmless: the health check sees it come back.

pc2.what: Later: a second VCU118 PC. Same as PC 1 when it arrives; then the license goes to vcu118:2.

tooling.title: Repo tooling
tooling.what: What keeps this view honest: the status file, test tags and a commit check. Not drawn on the diagram.
bullets: status.json next to this page holds every part's build status.
Every test is tagged with the part it covers; tools/status.py turns test results into tested or failing.
A pre-commit check refuses a commit that changes a part's code without updating its status.

more.title: More boards
bullets: Add a PC: sshd + driver, the kotl key, a registry entry, and one more Slurm license.
Different board types get their own license name (for example u250:2).
Servers without FPGAs can join for health and power monitoring only.

access.title: PC access (job keys)
access.what: Lets a job's owner, and their own FireSim, reach the board's PC for exactly as long as the job runs. No timers: access follows the job.
bullets: Job start: job.sh makes a fresh ed25519 key as the user (the private half never leaves their account). The launcher checks it is one bare ed25519 key and adds it for virtex-host through kotl-keys, with restrict,pty.

Job end (the command exits, kotl release, cancel or a guard): kotl-keys remove takes the key out and stops what the enabled adapters name (FireSim: its fsim* screens and FireSim-* drivers); in full lockdown it also ends every virtex-host process. Soft lockdown can't tell a job's ssh shells from password shells, so those stay (they can't log in again).
Backup: Slurm's epilog runs the same end step after every job, even if the launcher crashed. It is safe to run twice.
Only the board this job claimed gets the key. Outside a job, users can't reach any PC.

Lockdown mode (lockdown in /etc/kotl/kotl.conf): soft (now): password logins to virtex-host still work and other keys stay; the end step kills only this job's sessions and simulations. full (later): separate admin account, virtex-host key-only, end step kills every virtex-host process.

sys-ws.what: Everything Kotl adds on the workstation. Nothing outside these paths changes.
bullets: Packages: slurm-wlm, slurmdbd, munge, mariadb-server, expect (new · M1)
Accounts: system user kotl, group kotl-users (all regular users), Slurm's own slurm user (new · M1, deploy/accounts.sh)
/etc/slurm/slurm.conf: the single-node Slurm config: license, priority, ETA, KillWait, health check, Epilog (new · M1)
/etc/slurm/slurmdbd.conf: accounting daemon, using the MariaDB database slurm_acct_db (new · M1)
/etc/slurm/cgroup.conf: lets Slurm track every process of a job (new · M1)

/etc/kotl/kotl.conf: Kotl settings: lockdown mode, admin, PC account, idle time (new · M1)
/etc/systemd/system/kotl-notifier.{service,timer}: runs the notifier every minute, as kotl (new · M4)

/opt/kotl/kotl-status.vsix: the VS Code extension, for anyone to install (new · M5)

Slurm: the kotl account becomes an operator, so its guards can cancel a hung job (M2)

Services enabled: munge, mariadb, slurmdbd, slurmctld, slurmd (M1)

sys-users.what: Kotl changes nothing system-wide for users, and writes nothing into their Chipyard.
bullets: Their Chipyard and FireSim: read only. Kotl copies config_runtime.yaml into /srv/kotl/jobs/<job>/ and changes the copy.
Their home folder: nothing, unless they run kotl fetch (downloads results).
Their own PC: only the Claude Code plugin, if they install it (M5); it reaches the workstation with ssh $KOTL_SSH kotl ….

Per user, by their own command: kotl setup installs the Claude plugins and the VS Code extension in their own Claude Code and VS Code; on their own PC, ~/.kotl-client from the client bundle. Both have --undo.

top.what: A live screen of the boards, the queue and your own jobs, refreshed every 2 seconds. Plain terminal, nothing to install.
bullets: Boards: state, which job holds each one, its owner, time used and ETA.
Queue: who is waiting, the estimated start, and why (e.g. waiting for the board).
Your jobs: running and recent ones with their results. Keys: l logs, c cancel, r release a lease, f fetch results.
Reads the Kotl daemon's status file every second (no Slurm or launcher call); your history and notice texts come through the launcher's own checks every 10 s.

daemon.title: Kotl daemon (kotld)
daemon.what: Kotl's one always-running process: a small systemd service, run as kotl, that runs tasks on their own intervals. More tasks join it later.
bullets: Task: status (every 1 s): asks Slurm for the queue and the registry for the boards, and writes /run/kotl/status.json, readable by everyone. It holds only what squeue shows anyone, plus each user's count of unread notices (never their text).

Readers: kotl status, kotl top, the Claude band and the VS Code extension read that file instead of each asking Slurm and the launcher. One squeue a second in all, however many windows are open: no sudo, no Python start-up per viewer.
Cost: about 1–2 % of one core. The readers refresh every second for almost nothing.
If it stops: systemd restarts it within 2 s; meanwhile every reader falls back to asking Kotl directly (slower, same answers). A task's error never stops the daemon; it shows in kotl daemon.
Adding a task later: a small Task class in kotl/core/daemon.py with a name, an interval and a run().

nu-welcome.title: New to Kotl? Start here
nu-welcome.what: Kotl is the lab's queue for the FPGA boards. You never log in to a board's PC by hand: you ask Kotl for a board, it runs your work or gives you access, and frees the board the moment you're done.
bullets: 1 · Account: the admin adds you once.
2 · Setup: one command puts Kotl into your Claude Code and VS Code (on the workstation, or on your own PC).
3 · First job: kotl run --eta 5m -- hostname.
4 · Watch: the Kotl band in Claude Code, the Kotl panel in VS Code, or kotl top.
5 · Results, then your tools (FireSim via its adapter) and the house rules.
Use ◀ ▶ above to step through. Each step shows its commands here.

nu-account.title: 1 · Get an account
nu-account.what: The admin adds you to Kotl once. That gives you the kotl-users group, a Slurm account, and the one sudo rule Kotl needs.
bullets: Ask the admin to run: sudo deploy/accounts.sh add-user YOURNAME.

Then log in again (new ssh login; restart tmux with tmux kill-server; in VS Code: Remote-SSH: Kill VS Code Server on Host). A shell that started before you were added doesn't have the group, and Kotl will say "can't reach Kotl".
Check: id -nG lists kotl-users, and kotl status works without a password.

nu-setup-ws.title: 2a · Setup on the workstation
nu-setup-ws.what: One command installs Kotl into your Claude Code and VS Code. Safe to re-run (after updates too); --undo removes it.
bullets: Claude Code: the kotl plugin (Claude knows how to use the boards, asks before FireSim runs outside Kotl, shows the queue when a session starts) and kotl-band (a live line above the prompt).
VS Code: the Kotl extension (status bar and a Kotl panel). Connect VS Code to the workstation once first (Remote-SSH), then run kotl setup, then Developer: Reload Window.
Remove everything: kotl setup --undo.

nu-setup-pc.title: 2b · Setup on your own PC
nu-setup-pc.what: Working from your own machine: fetch a small bundle from the workstation and run its installer. It reads Kotl over ssh, so you need ssh to the workstation with a key.
bullets: The bundle holds both Claude plugins, the VS Code extension and an installer. It keeps its files in ~/.kotl-client, sets KOTL_SSH for Claude Code and tells VS Code the workstation's name.
Re-run it after updates. Remove: ~/.kotl-client/install.sh --undo.
Kotl commands then run on the workstation: ssh comparch kotl status; Claude does this for you.

nu-first.title: 3 · Your first job
nu-first.what: Hold a board while one command runs. The board is freed the moment it exits.
bullets: --eta is required: your honest estimate. It orders the queue and never kills the job; --max (default 2× ETA) stops a hung one.
Inside the job, $KOTL_PC is the board's PC and an ssh-agent holds a key that works only for this job.
Work by hand instead: kotl lease --eta 1h, then ssh vcu118-pc1, and always kotl release when done.

nu-watch.title: 4 · Watch the boards
nu-watch.what: Everything below reads the Kotl daemon's status file, refreshed every second.
bullets: Claude Code: the Kotl band above the prompt: who holds each board and their time of ETA, how many wait, your jobs with their ETA and place in line, unread notices. /kotl-band hide hides it.
VS Code: Kotl in the status bar (hover for the queue) and the Kotl panel (the chip icon on the left).
Terminal: kotl top (live; l logs, a attach, c cancel, r release, f fetch), kotl status, kotl notices.

nu-results.title: 5 · Results
nu-results.what: Every job leaves a folder only you can read, kept 30 days.
bullets: kotl logs JOB -f follows a running job's output.
kotl fetch JOB unpacks status.json, output.log, launcher.log and outputs/ into kotl-results/JOB/. Read status.json first.
kotl history lists your jobs and results; kotl notices has ETA, start-time and board notices.

nu-firesim.title: 6 · Your tools (FireSim)
nu-firesim.what: Any tool runs inside kotl run unchanged. FireSim, the lab's main one, has an adapter; here is how to run it.
bullets: Your Chipyard on your own PC? Build there (firesim builddriver, your workload), pack the run with ~/.kotl-client/adapters/firesim/kotl-firesim-pack -c CFG --out ~/kotl-runs/NAME, copy it with rsync to the workstation, then kotl run --eta 20m -- /opt/kotl/adapters/firesim/run-package.sh kotl-runs/NAME. One simulation, no network. Claude does these steps for you (the kotl-firesim skill).
Your Chipyard on the workstation? Run FireSim itself inside kotl run, as below.
In a shell with your Chipyard environment active (source env.sh, sourceme-manager.sh --skip-ssh-setup), and not Kotl's test venv (deactivate first).
The workload must power off by itself (FireMarshal run/command, or poweroff); otherwise --max ends the job.
This PC's glibc is older than the workstation's: remove FireSim's bundled glibc after infrasetup, e.g. with /opt/kotl/adapters/firesim/firesim-smoke.sh --use-pc-glibc.
Print KOTL RESULT: PASS or FAIL from the uartlog for an honest result.

nu-rules.title: 7 · House rules
nu-rules.what: The boards are shared; these keep them fair and working.
bullets: Never use a board outside Kotl: no plain firesim infrasetup/runworkload, no ssh to an FPGA PC without a lease.
Give an honest ETA; it's what everyone's start estimates are built on.
Release a lease the moment you're done (kotl release); idle leases are ended after 30 minutes anyway.
Problems with a board: kotl board list shows its health; tell the admin.

job.title: Your job
job.what: Whatever you run on a board: a test script, a bitstream load, a simulation, by hand during a lease. Kotl doesn't install, wrap or change your tools: it holds a board while your command runs, and frees it when it exits.
bullets: Batch: kotl run --eta T -- COMMAND. The board is held while the command runs and freed the moment it exits.
By hand: kotl lease --eta T, then ssh vcu118-pc1; kotl release when done.

Reaching the board's PC: inside the job your command has an ssh-agent holding only the job key, plus KOTL_JOB, KOTL_BOARD and KOTL_PC. Tools that use ssh (FireSim's run farm, rsync, your scripts) work unchanged.
Result: exit code 0 is succeeded; a line KOTL RESULT: PASS or FAIL in the output sets passed/failed when the exit code can't tell.
The exit plan: the command must end by itself (or the lease be released); --max (default 2× ETA) stops a hung one.
Tool-specific care (driver checks, cleanup, the console) comes from that tool's adapter. FireSim's is the first.

notes.title: Lab notes
notes.what: What the lab knows about running each tool on its boards: how the PCs are set up, what works together, every run Kotl saw and what it used, and free notes. Any Claude session (or person) reads them before a run and adds what it learned. Kept by Kotl on the workstation, at paths that never change.
bullets: Where: /srv/kotl/notes/: INDEX.md, general/ (setup.md, notes.md) and one folder per enabled adapter (firesim/: setup.md, compatible.md, runs.md, notes.md). Everyone on the workstation can read them; only Kotl writes, so every change has a date and an author. Not in git (they hold people's names and lab details); uninstall keeps them, --purge removes them.

Run lines, by Kotl: when a kotl run of a tool ends (passed, succeeded, failed, over_max or idle; not cancelled), the end step adds one line to that tool's runs.md: ok/FAIL, date, job, who, board, time, result, what it used, the command. A tool's run is one its adapter recognises (FireSim: the command mentions firesim) or one that says KOTL FACT: tool=…. runs.md keeps its last 500 lines; older ones go to runs-old.md.

What a run used comes from the adapter's facts lines, run by job.sh as the user in the job's folder as the command ends (at most 20 s; FireSim: its and Chipyard's commits, the hardware config, its bitstream and the workload, read-only). A command that prints KOTL FACT: key=value lines describes itself instead (the FireSim test package does, from its MANIFEST).

Curated pages: setup.md and compatible.md start from the adapter's text and are replaced with kotl notes set; the old page is kept in .history/ (kotl notes history TOOL). notes.md only grows: kotl notes add adds a dated, signed line.

Claude finds them through the general skill (a table: tool, its skill, its notes), the tool's own skill (FireSim's says: read the notes, compare the run with the last good ones, then run, then add), the session-start line and /etc/claude-code/CLAUDE.md.

jobsh.name: job.sh
jobsh.desc: What Slurm runs for every Kotl job, as the user: start (claim), your command, end step
jobsh.body:
#!/bin/bash
# managed by kotl (deploy/kotl/install.sh)
# What Slurm runs for every Kotl job, as the submitting user, inside their job:
#   1) the launcher (as kotl) checks the job is yours, claims a board, starts the guards
#   2) your command runs as you; its output goes to the job's output.log
#   3) the end step: frees the board and writes status.json (Slurm's epilog repeats it)
# Settings come from the kotl CLI: KOTL_MODE (run|lease), KOTL_MAX and KOTL_IDLE (seconds).
set -u
JOB=${SLURM_JOB_ID:?not inside a Slurm job}
read -r -a LAUNCH <<<"${KOTL_LAUNCH:-sudo -n -u kotl /opt/kotl/launch}"

"${LAUNCH[@]}" start "$JOB" --mode "${KOTL_MODE:-run}" \
  ${KOTL_MAX:+--max "$KOTL_MAX"} ${KOTL_IDLE:+--idle "$KOTL_IDLE"} --command "$*" || exit 1

stopping=0 pid=""
on_stop() { stopping=1; [ -n "$pid" ] && kill -TERM "$pid" 2>/dev/null; }
trap on_stop TERM INT HUP

# your command's output goes through a pipe to the launcher, which owns the log file
fifo=$(mktemp -u "${TMPDIR:-/tmp}/kotl-$JOB.XXXXXX")
mkfifo -m 600 "$fifo"
"${LAUNCH[@]}" log "$JOB" <"$fifo" &
logpid=$!
"$@" >"$fifo" 2>&1 &
pid=$!
rc=0
while :; do
  wait "$pid"; rc=$?
  kill -0 "$pid" 2>/dev/null || break   # wait returns early when a signal arrives
done
# let the log writer drain (at most 10 s, in case something still holds the pipe open)
for _ in $(seq 1 50); do kill -0 "$logpid" 2>/dev/null || break; sleep 0.2; done
kill "$logpid" 2>/dev/null; wait "$logpid" 2>/dev/null
rm -f "$fifo"

if [ "$stopping" = 1 ]; then
  "${LAUNCH[@]}" end "$JOB" --signal
else
  "${LAUNCH[@]}" end "$JOB" --rc "$rc"
fi
exit "$rc"

skill.name: SKILL.md
skill.desc: The general skill: kotl run / lease with an ETA and an exit plan, fetch then read status.json, the lab notes, and a table pointing to each tool's own skill (FireSim: kotl-firesim)
skill.body:
---
name: kotl
description: Use the lab's FPGA boards (VCU118) through Kotl, the lab's board queue. Use whenever a task runs anything on an FPGA board or its PC (FireSim infrasetup/runworkload, a bitstream, a driver test, ssh to an FPGA PC), or when the person asks about the board queue, their Kotl jobs, results, logs, notices or the lab notes (what worked before). For FireSim also read the kotl-firesim skill.
---

# Kotl: the lab's FPGA board queue

The FPGA boards are shared. Kotl queues every use of a board through Slurm, gives the job SSH
access to the board's PC only while it runs, and frees the board the moment the job ends.
**Never use a board outside Kotl** (no plain `firesim infrasetup`/`runworkload`, no direct ssh to
an FPGA PC without a lease): it can break someone else's run.

## Where to run `kotl`

- On the workstation (`command -v kotl` finds it): run `kotl ...` directly.
- On a user's own PC: run it over ssh, `ssh "$KOTL_SSH" 'cd <folder> && kotl ...'`.
  `KOTL_SSH` is the workstation's ssh name (set in `~/.claude/settings.json` under `env`). If it
  is unset, ask the person for it. Files and folders must exist on the workstation.

## Every job needs an ETA and an exit plan

- `--eta` is required: your honest estimate. It only orders the queue; it never kills the job.
- `--max` (default 2x ETA) stops a hung job. Set it when a run might legitimately take longer.
- The job must end by itself: a command that exits, or a lease that is released.

## Run a command on a board: `kotl run` (preferred)

The board is held while the command runs and freed the moment it exits.

```sh
kotl run --eta 30m -- <command>
```

- Inside the job, the command has `KOTL_JOB`, `KOTL_BOARD`, `KOTL_PC` (user@address of the board's
  PC) and an ssh-agent holding only the job key: `ssh "$KOTL_PC" ...` works, FireSim's own ssh too.
- Exit code 0 = `succeeded`. A line `KOTL RESULT: PASS` or `KOTL RESULT: FAIL` in the output sets
  `passed`/`failed` instead. Print one when the exit code alone can't tell (the tool's skill says
  how).
- `kotl run` waits and streams the output. For a long run, add `--no-wait` (it prints the job
  number), then follow with `kotl logs JOB -f` or check `kotl status`. Run long waits in the
  background rather than blocking the conversation.

## Tools on the boards: each has its own skill, and lab notes

Kotl itself is generic: it queues the board and gives the job access. What one tool needs lives
in that tool's adapter, and each adapter brings a skill. Before running a tool on a board, read its
skill (it is installed next to this one) and its lab notes.

| Tool | Skill | Lab notes |
| --- | --- | --- |
| FireSim | `kotl-firesim` | `kotl notes firesim` |
| anything else (a driver test, `ls` on the PC) | this skill | `kotl notes general` |

## Lab notes: what the lab knows, kept by Kotl

`/srv/kotl/notes/` on the workstation holds what worked before, per tool. The paths never change:

```sh
kotl notes                      # the index: every tool's pages, and its last good run
kotl notes firesim              # setup.md, compatible.md, the latest runs, notes.md
kotl notes firesim runs.md      # one page, whole
kotl notes add firesim "text"   # a dated, signed note: what you learned, what to avoid
```

- **Read them before a run**: `setup.md` (what the board's PC has), `compatible.md` (what works
  together), `runs.md` (every run Kotl saw, `ok`/`FAIL`, with what it used), `notes.md` (free
  notes). Compare what the person is about to run with the last good runs, and say so if it
  differs (another commit, config or bitstream) before using the queue.
- **Kotl adds the run line itself** when a `kotl run` of a tool ends. A command can describe
  itself with `KOTL FACT: key=value` lines in its output (they replace what the adapter finds).
- **Add a note** when you learn something the next person needs: a fix, a known-bad combination,
  a step that was missing. One or two lines, facts only. Runs done in a lease get no automatic
  line: add one.
- `kotl notes set TOOL setup.md|compatible.md < file` replaces a curated page (the old one is kept;
  `kotl notes history TOOL`). Change these only with facts from runs, and tell the person.
- Lab facts in the notes come from the lab; don't invent them.

## Work by hand: `kotl lease`

```sh
kotl lease --eta 1h        # waits for a board, then prints how to reach it
ssh <board>                # e.g. ssh vcu118-pc1: uses the lease's job key
kotl attach                # FireSim's console (Ctrl-a d detaches)
kotl release               # ALWAYS release when done
```

A lease ends on `kotl release`, after 30 minutes with nothing of yours running on the PC, or at
`--max`. If you start a lease for the person, release it when the work is done.

## Check, follow, fetch

| Need | Command |
| --- | --- |
| queue, boards, unread notices | `kotl status` (live view for a person: `kotl top`) |
| your past jobs and results | `kotl history` |
| output of a job | `kotl logs JOB` (`-f` follows a running one) |
| everything a job left | `kotl fetch JOB` -> `kotl-results/JOB/` with `status.json`, `output.log`, `launcher.log`, `outputs/` |
| cancel your job | `kotl cancel JOB` |
| notices (ETA passed, start slipped, board down/up) | `kotl notices` (marks them read) |

After a job ends: fetch it, read `status.json` first (`result`, `rc`, `reason`), then
`output.log`, then `launcher.log` (what Kotl did: key added/removed, guards, end). Report the
result, how long it took against the ETA, and anything odd.

## Results

`passed` / `failed` (KOTL RESULT line), `succeeded` / `failed` (exit code), `over_max` (the --max
guard stopped it), `idle` (a lease with nothing running), `released`, `cancelled`, `killed`
(ended by Slurm's backup), `no_access` (the board's PC couldn't be reached).

## A board that is busy, or a run that stopped

- Signs that a machine or board is Kotl's: `kotl` on the workstation's PATH, files on an FPGA PC
  that start with "managed by kotl" (`/usr/local/bin/kotl-*`, `/etc/sudoers.d/kotl*`), and
  `kotl-job-N` keys in the board account's `~/.ssh/authorized_keys`. If you see them, every use of
  that board goes through Kotl.
- A FireSim `fsim*` screen or `FireSim-*` driver on a board's PC that isn't your job's is someone
  else's work, or work outside Kotl. **Never stop it.** Tell the person who seems to run it, for
  how long, and that it is outside Kotl. `kotl board list` and `kotl status` show the same.
- Kotl itself never stops work it didn't start: a job's end step stops only what started during
  that job. If the person's run outside Kotl stopped anyway, look at `kotl status` and
  `kotl history` (a Kotl job may have taken the board), then move the run into `kotl run`.

## Don'ts

- Don't run FireSim or touch an FPGA PC outside a Kotl job or lease.
- Don't stop FireSim, screens or processes on a board's PC that aren't your own job's.
- Don't cancel other people's jobs (Kotl won't let you anyway).
- Don't leave a lease running: release it.
- Don't start a tool's run without reading its lab notes first, and don't leave what you learned
  out of them.
- Don't guess an ETA of hours for a minutes-long run: ETAs order the queue for everyone.

kotlkeys.desc: The only Kotl code on a PC: adds and removes job keys for virtex-host; stops what the adapters name. Knows no tool
kotlkeys.body:
#!/bin/sh
# managed by kotl (deploy/pc/setup.sh). Installed on each FPGA PC as /usr/local/bin/kotl-keys.
# Runs as the PC's board account (virtex-host), started by the kotl account through sudo.
# Generic: what a tool leaves running (FireSim's screens and drivers) is named by the workstation's
# adapters, as --screen/--proc arguments; this script knows no tool.
#
#   kotl-keys add JOB 'ssh-ed25519 KEY'   let this job's key in (no forwarding; a terminal is allowed)
#   kotl-keys remove JOB [soft|full] [--max-age SECONDS] [--screen PREFIX]... [--proc PREFIX]...
#                                         take the key out, quit the named screen sessions and stop
#                                         the named processes (by process name); with --max-age only
#                                         those that started during the job (younger than SECONDS),
#                                         older ones are left and reported. Full lockdown ends every
#                                         process of this account
#   kotl-keys list                        jobs whose keys are in
#   kotl-keys busy [--proc PREFIX]...     "busy: NAME, NAME; for SECONDS" if remote work of this account runs here
#                                         (SSH sessions and what they started, screen, tmux, and the
#                                         named processes; not a local desktop login), else "idle":
#                                         the lease idle guard and the health check's warning
#
# Only lines ending in "kotl-job-<JOB>" are ever touched; every other key stays.
set -eu
umask 077
ME=$(id -un)
HOMEDIR=$(getent passwd "$ME" | cut -d: -f6)
# tests only: sudo resets the environment, so these can't be set in real use
HOMEDIR=${KOTL_KEYS_TEST_HOME:-$HOMEDIR}
AK="$HOMEDIR/.ssh/authorized_keys"
mkdir -p "$HOMEDIR/.ssh"
[ -e "$AK" ] || : >"$AK"

die() { echo "kotl-keys: $*" >&2; exit 2; }
job_ok() { case "${1:-}" in ''|*[!0-9]*) die "bad job id '${1:-}'" ;; esac; }
strip() {   # drop this job's lines, keep everything else and the file itself
  tmp=$(mktemp "$AK.XXXXXX")
  grep -v " kotl-job-$1\$" "$AK" >"$tmp" || true
  cat "$tmp" >"$AK"
  rm -f "$tmp"
}

# --screen/--proc NAME pairs after the fixed arguments; names are plain words only
SCREENS="" PROCS="" MAXAGE=""
names() {
  while [ $# -gt 0 ]; do
    case "$1" in
      --max-age)
        case "${2:-}" in ''|*[!0-9]*) die "bad --max-age '${2:-}'" ;; esac
        MAXAGE=$2; shift 2 ;;
      --screen|--proc)
        case "${2:-}" in ''|*[!A-Za-z0-9_.-]*) die "bad name '${2:-}' for $1" ;; esac
        if [ "$1" = --screen ]; then SCREENS="$SCREENS $2"; else PROCS="$PROCS $2"; fi
        shift 2 ;;
      *) die "unknown argument '$1'" ;;
    esac
  done
}

exec 9>"$HOMEDIR/.ssh/.kotl-keys.lock"
flock 9

case "${1:-}" in
  add)
    job_ok "${2:-}"
    printf '%s\n' "${3:-}" | grep -Eqx 'ssh-ed25519 [A-Za-z0-9+/]+={0,3}' || die "the key must be one ssh-ed25519 public key"
    strip "$2"
    printf 'restrict,pty %s kotl-job-%s\n' "$3" "$2" >>"$AK"
    chmod 600 "$AK"
    ;;
  remove)
    job_ok "${2:-}"
    JOB=$2 MODE=soft
    shift 2
    case "${1:-}" in soft|full) MODE=$1; shift ;; esac
    names "$@"
    strip "$JOB"
    [ -z "${KOTL_KEYS_TEST_HOME:-}" ] || { echo "would stop screens:${SCREENS:- none} procs:${PROCS:- none} max-age:${MAXAGE:-none}"; exit 0; }
    # stop what the adapters named: their screen sessions, then their processes (matched by
    # process name, never by command line: this script's own arguments name them too).
    # With --max-age, only what started during the job; older work isn't this job's.
    young() { [ -z "$MAXAGE" ] || [ "$(ps -o etimes= -p "$1" 2>/dev/null | tr -d ' ')" -le "$MAXAGE" ] 2>/dev/null; }
    stopped="" left=""
    for p in $SCREENS; do
      for s in $(screen -ls 2>/dev/null | awk -v p="$p" '$1 ~ "^[0-9]+\\." p { print $1 }'); do
        if young "${s%%.*}"; then screen -S "$s" -X quit 2>/dev/null || true; stopped="$stopped screen:$s"
        else left="$left screen:$s"; fi
      done
    done
    for p in $PROCS; do
      for pid in $(ps -u "$ME" -o pid=,comm= | awk -v p="$p" -v me="$$" '$1 != me && index($2, p) == 1 { print $1 }'); do
        if young "$pid"; then kill "$pid" 2>/dev/null || true; stopped="$stopped $pid"
        else left="$left $pid"; fi
      done
    done
    echo "stopped:${stopped:- nothing}; left running (older than this job, outside Kotl):${left:- nothing}"
    if [ "$MODE" = full ]; then
      exec pkill -KILL -u "$ME"   # full lockdown: nothing of this account outlives the job
    fi
    ;;
  busy)
    # Remote work only: processes in this account's SSH sessions, plus screen sessions, tmux
    # servers and the named processes (they outlive the ssh that started them). The PC's own desktop
    # login, if it runs as this account, isn't counted. This check itself isn't either.
    shift
    names "$@"
    mysid=$(ps -o sid= -p $$ | tr -d ' ')
    sshsids=$(ps -u "$ME" -o sid=,comm= | awk '$2 == "sshd" {print $1}' | sort -u | tr '\n' ' ')
    counted=$(ps -u "$ME" -o sid=,etimes=,comm=,args= | awk -v me="$mysid" -v ss=" $sshsids" -v procs="$PROCS" '
        BEGIN { n = split(procs, pp, " ") }
        $1 == me { next }
        index(ss, " " $1 " ") || $3 == "screen" || $3 == "SCREEN" || $3 ~ /^tmux/ { print $2, $3; next }
        { for (i = 1; i <= n; i++) if (index($3, pp[i]) == 1 || index($0, " " pp[i]) || index($0, "/" pp[i])) { print $2, $3; next } }')
    found=$(printf '%s\n' "$counted" | awk 'NF { print $2 }' | sort | uniq -c | awk '{print $2 ($1 > 1 ? " x" $1 : "")}' | paste -sd, - | sed 's/,/, /g')
    oldest=$(printf '%s\n' "$counted" | awk 'NF && $1 > m { m = $1 } END { print m + 0 }')
    if [ -n "$found" ]; then echo "busy: $found; for $oldest"; else echo idle; fi
    ;;
  list)
    sed -n 's/.* kotl-job-\([0-9][0-9]*\)$/\1/p' "$AK"
    ;;
  *) die "usage: kotl-keys add JOB KEY | remove JOB [soft|full] [--screen P]... [--proc P]... | list | busy [--proc P]..." ;;
esac

xdmareload.desc: FireSim adapter: the health check's one driver reload on an idle board, loading XDMA exactly as FireSim does (poll_mode=1)
xdmareload.body:
#!/bin/sh
# managed by kotl (deploy/adapters/firesim/pc-setup.sh). FireSim adapter. Installed on each FPGA PC as /usr/local/bin/kotl-xdma-reload.
# Kotl's health check runs it (as root, through one sudoers line, with no arguments) when the
# XDMA driver isn't loaded on an IDLE board: one attempt to reload it. It changes nothing else.
#
# It loads the driver exactly as FireSim's own infrasetup does (the same module, poll_mode=1):
# FireSim skips its own load when xdma is already loaded, so a driver loaded any other way
# (e.g. a plain `modprobe xdma`) would be the one FireSim runs on, and its simulation driver
# then can't find the card ("xdma_id != -1").
set -eu
KO="/lib/modules/$(uname -r)/extra/xdma.ko"
rmmod xdma 2>/dev/null || true
if [ -f "$KO" ]; then
  insmod "$KO" poll_mode=1
else
  modprobe xdma poll_mode=1
fi
lsmod | grep -q '^xdma '
echo "kotl-xdma-reload: xdma loaded (poll_mode=$(cat /sys/module/xdma/parameters/poll_mode 2>/dev/null || echo ?))"

#!/bin/sh
# managed by kotl (deploy/client/install.sh)
# Kotl on your own PC: the Claude Code plugins (kotl, kotl-band) and the VS Code extension,
# reading Kotl over ssh from the workstation. Get this folder with:
#
#   ssh <workstation> kotl client-bundle > kotl-client.tar && tar xf kotl-client.tar
#   ./kotl-client/install.sh [--ssh <workstation ssh name>]     install (re-run after updates)
#   ./kotl-client/install.sh --undo                             remove it all again
#
# It keeps its files in ~/.kotl-client (with the adapters' tools for your own builds, e.g.
# ~/.kotl-client/adapters/firesim/kotl-firesim-pack), sets KOTL_SSH for Claude Code (~/.claude/settings.json)
# and tells the VS Code extension the workstation's name (~/.kotl-client/ssh). Needs ssh to the
# workstation with a key (no password prompt), python3, and Claude Code and/or VS Code.
set -u
HERE=$(cd "$(dirname "$0")" && pwd)
DEST="$HOME/.kotl-client"
SSH=$(cat "$HERE/workstation" 2>/dev/null || true)
UNDO=0
while [ $# -gt 0 ]; do
  case "$1" in
    --ssh) SSH=${2:-}; shift ;;
    --undo) UNDO=1 ;;
    -h|--help) sed -n '3,13p' "$0" | sed 's/^# \{0,1\}//'; exit 0 ;;
    *) echo "unknown option $1" >&2; exit 2 ;;
  esac
  shift
done

settings_env() {  # settings_env set NAME VALUE | settings_env unset NAME   (~/.claude/settings.json)
  python3 - "$@" <<'PY'
import json, os, sys
p = os.path.expanduser("~/.claude/settings.json")
os.makedirs(os.path.dirname(p), exist_ok=True)
try:
    s = json.load(open(p))
except (OSError, ValueError):
    s = {}
env = s.setdefault("env", {})
if sys.argv[1] == "set":
    env[sys.argv[2]] = sys.argv[3]
else:
    env.pop(sys.argv[2], None)
    if not env:
        s.pop("env")
json.dump(s, open(p, "w"), indent=2)
PY
}

if [ "$UNDO" = 1 ]; then
  if command -v claude >/dev/null; then
    claude plugin uninstall kotl@kotl >/dev/null 2>&1 && echo "- Claude Code: kotl removed"
    claude plugin uninstall kotl-band@kotl >/dev/null 2>&1 && echo "- Claude Code: kotl-band removed"
    claude plugin marketplace remove kotl >/dev/null 2>&1 && echo "- Claude Code: marketplace removed"
    settings_env unset KOTL_SSH && echo "- Claude Code: KOTL_SSH removed"
  fi
  if command -v code >/dev/null; then
    code --uninstall-extension kotl.kotl-status >/dev/null 2>&1 && echo "- VS Code: extension removed"
  fi
  rm -rf "$DEST" && echo "- removed $DEST"
  exit 0
fi

[ -n "$SSH" ] || { echo "give the workstation's ssh name: --ssh NAME" >&2; exit 2; }
echo "Workstation: $SSH"
if ssh -o BatchMode=yes -o ConnectTimeout=5 "$SSH" kotl status --json >/dev/null 2>&1; then
  echo "- ssh $SSH kotl: works"
else
  echo "! ssh $SSH kotl status failed: check you can ssh there with a key, and that you are in kotl-users"
fi

# a stable copy: Claude Code reads the plugins from this folder
if [ "$HERE" != "$DEST" ]; then mkdir -p "$(dirname "$DEST")"; rm -rf "$DEST"; cp -R "$HERE" "$DEST"; fi
printf '%s\n' "$SSH" >"$DEST/ssh"

if command -v claude >/dev/null; then
  claude plugin marketplace list 2>/dev/null | grep -q kotl || claude plugin marketplace add "$DEST" >/dev/null
  for p in kotl@kotl kotl-band@kotl; do
    claude plugin install "$p" >/dev/null 2>&1 || true
    echo "- Claude Code: $p installed"
  done
  settings_env set KOTL_SSH "$SSH" && echo "- Claude Code: KOTL_SSH=$SSH"
else
  echo "- Claude Code: not installed here; skipped"
fi

if command -v code >/dev/null; then
  code --install-extension "$DEST/kotl-status.vsix" --force >/dev/null && echo "- VS Code: extension installed (reload the window)"
else
  echo "- VS Code: the 'code' command isn't on PATH; skipped (in VS Code: Shell Command: Install 'code' command, then re-run)"
fi
[ -x "$DEST/adapters/firesim/kotl-firesim-pack" ] && echo "- FireSim: $DEST/adapters/firesim/kotl-firesim-pack packs a run of your own build for the boards"
echo "Done. Start a new Claude Code session; in VS Code, Kotl is in the status bar and the Kotl panel."

fsadapter.name: __init__.py
fsadapter.desc: The FireSim adapter: its checks, repair, cleanup names and console
fsadapter.body:
"""FireSim adapter: what Kotl needs to know so users can run their own FireSim on a board.

Users run FireSim unchanged inside `kotl run` / `kotl lease`; this adapter only adds:

  checks    XDMA driver loaded (failure); glibc on the PC vs the workstation (warning: drivers
            built here won't start on an older glibc)
  repair    one XDMA reload on an IDLE board (kotl-xdma-reload on the PC, loading it exactly as
            FireSim's infrasetup does, poll_mode=1). Never while a job holds the board: FireSim
            unloads and reloads XDMA itself during infrasetup.
  end step  quit FireSim's screen sessions (fsim*) and stop its drivers (FireSim-*); then, as root,
            kotl-firesim-stop: FireSim starts its driver through sudo, so the driver runs as
            root and the board account can't stop it. Both stop only what started during the
            job (the job's age is passed); older FireSim work on the PC isn't the job's: it is
            left running and reported (who, how long, outside Kotl)
  idle      FireSim-* processes count as work for the lease idle guard
  console   `kotl attach` opens screen session fsim0
  notes     a job whose command mentions firesim is a FireSim run: when it ends, its line in the
            lab notes (firesim/runs.md) carries the FireSim and Chipyard commits, the hardware
            config, its bitstream and the workload, read from the user's FireSim (FACTS, run as
            the user). The pages start from SEED until someone writes them

Its PC part is deploy/adapters/firesim/ (kotl-xdma-reload, kotl-firesim-stop and their install). Later, admin only:
flash a known-good bitstream, recover a board.
"""
import re
import subprocess

from kotl import ssh as ssh_mod
from kotl.adapters import Adapter

RELOAD = "/usr/local/bin/kotl-xdma-reload"

# run as the user in the job's folder when a FireSim run ends: key=value lines for runs.md
FACTS = r"""
echo tool=firesim
fs=$(command -v firesim 2>/dev/null) || exit 0
dep=$(cd "$(dirname "$(readlink -f "$fs")")" 2>/dev/null && pwd) || exit 0
ver() {
  c=$(git -C "$1" rev-parse --short=10 HEAD 2>/dev/null) || return 1   # read-only: no index refresh
  git --no-optional-locks -C "$1" diff --quiet --ignore-submodules HEAD 2>/dev/null || c="$c+changes"
  echo "$c"
}
v=$(ver "$dep/..") && echo "firesim=$v"
cy=$(git -C "$dep/.." rev-parse --show-superproject-working-tree 2>/dev/null)
[ -n "$cy" ] && v=$(ver "$cy") && echo "chipyard=$v"
# a FireSim config given in the command (-c/--runtimeconfigfile, -a/--hwdbconfigfile: *.yaml)
arg() {
  set -f; set -- $KOTL_COMMAND; set +f
  while [ $# -gt 1 ]; do
    case "$1" in "$A"|"$B") case "$2" in *.yaml|*.yml) echo "$2"; return ;; esac ;; esac
    shift
  done
}
val() { sed -n "s/^[[:space:]]*$1:[[:space:]]*//p" "$2" 2>/dev/null | sed 's/[[:space:]]*#.*//; s/["'"'"']//g' | head -n 1; }
A=-c B=--runtimeconfigfile rt=$(arg); rt=${rt:-$dep/config_runtime.yaml}
A=-a B=--hwdbconfigfile hwdb=$(arg); hwdb=${hwdb:-$dep/config_hwdb.yaml}
[ "$rt" = "$dep/config_runtime.yaml" ] || echo "runtime_config=$rt"
hw=$(val default_hw_config "$rt"); [ -n "$hw" ] && echo "hw_config=$hw"
wl=$(val workload_name "$rt"); [ -n "$wl" ] && echo "workload=$wl"
if [ -n "$hw" ]; then
  bit=$(awk -v h="$hw:" '$1 == h { f = 1; next } f && /^[^[:space:]#]/ { f = 0 }
                         f && $1 == "bitstream_tar:" { print $2; exit }' "$hwdb" 2>/dev/null)
  bit=${bit#file://}
  [ -n "$bit" ] && echo "bitstream=$(basename "$(dirname "$bit")")"
fi
true
"""

SEED = {
    "setup.md": """# FireSim: setup

What the boards' PCs have for FireSim, and what a run needs. Correct it when something changes:
kotl notes set firesim setup.md < file (the old page is kept in .history/).

## Every board's PC (Kotl's health check watches these)

- XDMA driver loaded, poll_mode=1 (Kotl reloads it on an idle board if it's missing)
- xvsec driver and xvsecctl, to flash the bitstream (what FireSim's infrasetup does)
- the board account can use sudo without a password (FireSim runs its driver through sudo)
- glibc: `kotl board list` warns when the PC's differs from the workstation's; then remove
  FireSim's bundled glibc on the PC after infrasetup (/opt/kotl/adapters/firesim/firesim-smoke.sh
  --use-pc-glibc)

## Not written yet

- the boards (type, PC, shell/bitstream flashed at boot)
- the Vivado, XDMA and FireSim versions the PCs are set up for
- the lab's FireSim test package (a known-good bitstream and driver): where it is
""",
    "compatible.md": """# FireSim: what works together

Known-good combinations on these boards (FireSim and Chipyard commits, hardware config and
bitstream, driver, workload), and known-bad ones with the symptom. The latest runs are in
runs.md: each line has what that run used. Correct this page with
kotl notes set firesim compatible.md < file.

## Known good

(none written yet: see the ok lines in runs.md)

## Known bad

(none written yet)

## Watch out: the FireSim version

The board's PC was set up (XDMA driver, poll_mode=1, xvsec) for one FireSim version. A design
built with a much newer or older FireSim may expect another XDMA driver, and nothing checks
that before the run: it shows as a flash or driver-start failure. Compare the run's firesim=
commit with the ok lines in runs.md; the first run on a new FireSim version, pass or fail,
belongs in this page.
""",
}
STOP = "/usr/local/bin/kotl-firesim-stop"


def glibc_line(text):
    """First line of `ldd --version`, e.g. 'ldd (Ubuntu GLIBC 2.39-0ubuntu8.12) 2.39'."""
    return (text or "").strip().splitlines()[0].strip() if (text or "").strip() else ""


def glibc_version(line):
    """The distro's full glibc version from that line ('2.39-0ubuntu8.12'), or the plain version."""
    m = re.search(r"GLIBC ([^)\s]+)\)", line)       # Ubuntu/Debian: the full package version
    if m:
        return m.group(1)
    return line.split()[-1] if line else ""


def local_glibc():
    r = subprocess.run(["ldd", "--version"], capture_output=True, text=True)
    return glibc_version(glibc_line(r.stdout))


def glibc_warning(here, there):
    if not there or there == here:
        return None
    base_here, base_there = here.split("-")[0], there.split("-")[0]
    if base_here != base_there:
        fix = (f"the PC has an older glibc release ({base_there} vs {base_here}), which a package update "
               f"can't close: remove the bundled glibc after infrasetup (/opt/kotl/adapters/firesim/firesim-smoke.sh "
               f"--use-pc-glibc), or bring the PC to the workstation's OS release")
    else:
        fix = "upgrade libc6 on the PC to match, or remove the bundled glibc after infrasetup (--use-pc-glibc)"
    return (f"glibc differs: workstation {here}, PC {there}. FireSim drivers built on the "
            f"workstation won't start on this PC as they are: {fix}")


class FireSim(Adapter):
    name = "firesim"
    probe = ('echo "xdma=$(lsmod 2>/dev/null | grep -o "^xdma ")"; '
             'echo "glibc=$(ldd --version 2>/dev/null | head -n 1)"')
    stop_screens = ("fsim",)
    stop_procs = ("FireSim-",)
    work_procs = ("FireSim-",)
    console = "fsim0"
    title = "FireSim"
    notes_seed = SEED
    facts = FACTS

    def is_run(self, command):
        return bool(re.search(r"firesim", command, re.I))

    def end_commands(self, age):
        return [["sudo", "-n", STOP] + ([str(int(age))] if age is not None else [])]
    XDMA = "XDMA driver not loaded (lsmod)"

    def __init__(self, here=None):
        self._here = here

    @property
    def here(self):
        if self._here is None:
            self._here = local_glibc()
        return self._here

    def failures(self, p):
        return [] if p.get("xdma") else [self.XDMA]

    def warnings(self, p):
        w = glibc_warning(self.here, glibc_version(p.get("glibc", "")))
        return [w] if w else []

    def repair(self, board, ssh, failures):
        if self.XDMA not in failures:
            return None
        try:
            ssh.run(board["host"], ["sudo", "-n", RELOAD], timeout=120)
            return "tried one XDMA driver reload"
        except ssh_mod.SSHError as e:
            return f"XDMA driver reload failed: {e}"

fspcsetup.name: pc-setup.sh
fspcsetup.desc: Installs (or --undo removes) the adapter's PC part: kotl-xdma-reload and its sudoers line
fspcsetup.body:
#!/usr/bin/env bash
# FireSim adapter, the PC part. Runs ON an FPGA PC, as root, with kotl-xdma-reload and
# kotl-firesim-stop copied next to it.
#
#   sudo bash pc-setup.sh            installs both in /usr/local/bin with one sudoers line each:
#                                    kotl may run only that script, as root, with no arguments
#                                    kotl-xdma-reload:  the health check's one XDMA reload (idle board)
#                                    kotl-firesim-stop: the end step stops FireSim's root driver
#                                    (it may also pass the job's age: a number, the script checks it)
#   sudo bash pc-setup.sh --undo     removes them
#
# Needs Kotl's own PC setup first (deploy/pc/setup.sh: the kotl account). Add --dry-run to preview.
set -euo pipefail

HERE=$(cd "$(dirname "$0")" && pwd)
DRY=0 ACTION=install
say() { printf 'kotl-pc (firesim): %s\n' "$*"; }
die() { printf 'kotl-pc (firesim): error: %s\n' "$*" >&2; exit 1; }
run() { if [ "$DRY" = 1 ]; then printf 'would run: %s\n' "$*"; else "$@"; fi; }

while [ $# -gt 0 ]; do
  case "$1" in
    --dry-run) DRY=1 ;;
    --undo) ACTION=undo ;;
    -h|--help) sed -n '2,12p' "$0" | sed 's/^# \{0,1\}//'; exit 0 ;;
    *) die "unknown option $1" ;;
  esac
  shift
done
[ "$DRY" = 1 ] || [ "$(id -u)" = 0 ] || die "run as root (sudo bash $0), or add --dry-run"

if [ "$ACTION" = undo ]; then
  run rm -f /usr/local/bin/kotl-xdma-reload /etc/sudoers.d/kotl-driver
  run rm -f /usr/local/bin/kotl-firesim-stop /etc/sudoers.d/kotl-firesim-stop
  say "removed kotl-xdma-reload, kotl-firesim-stop and their sudoers lines"
  exit 0
fi

# install_helper NAME SUDOERS-FILE [any]: /usr/local/bin/NAME, and "kotl may run it as root" with
# no arguments (or, with "any", also with arguments, which the script itself checks)
install_helper() {
  local src="$HERE/$1" rule
  [ -f "$src" ] || die "copy $1 next to this script"
  head -n 3 "$src" | grep -q 'managed by kotl' || die "$src is not Kotl's $1"
  run install -m 755 -o root -g root "$src" "/usr/local/bin/$1"
  rule="kotl ALL=(root) NOPASSWD: /usr/local/bin/$1 \"\""
  [ "${3:-}" = any ] && rule="kotl ALL=(root) NOPASSWD: /usr/local/bin/$1 \"\", /usr/local/bin/$1 [0-9]*"
  if [ "$DRY" = 1 ]; then
    say "would write /etc/sudoers.d/$2 (440): $rule"
  else
    tmp=$(mktemp)
    printf '# managed by kotl (deploy/adapters/firesim/pc-setup.sh)\n%s\n' "$rule" >"$tmp"
    visudo -cf "$tmp" >/dev/null || { rm -f "$tmp"; die "sudoers line failed visudo"; }
    install -m 440 -o root -g root "$tmp" "/etc/sudoers.d/$2"
    rm -f "$tmp"
  fi
  say "$1 installed; kotl may run it as root$([ "${3:-}" = any ] && echo ", with a number of seconds or nothing" || echo ", with no arguments")"
}

modinfo xdma >/dev/null 2>&1 || [ -f "/lib/modules/$(uname -r)/extra/xdma.ko" ] ||
  say "WARNING: no xdma module found here, so the reload can't work"
install_helper kotl-xdma-reload kotl-driver
install_helper kotl-firesim-stop kotl-firesim-stop any
